presenterNotes: Block 1: Emphasize the skewness of the chi‑square distribution. Show how to use both the table and Google Sheets for critical values. Note that two‑tailed critical values are not opposites.
Block 2: Walk through the test statistic carefully. The milk variance example is a good starting point. Remind students to square standard deviations.
Block 3: P‑values for chi‑square tests are easy with Google Sheets. The two‑tailed P‑value is not just double the right‑tail area.
Block 4: Real‑world examples from quality control motivate the test. Emphasize the normality assumption.
Block 5: The blueprint ties everything together. Encourage students to always check the direction of the test and use variances.

visuals.title: Finding Critical Values for a Chi‑Square Test

explanation: The [[kw:chi‑square test]] is used to test claims about a population variance $\sigma^2$ or standard deviation $\sigma$ when the population is [[imp:normally distributed]].
The critical value(s) depend on the test type and the significance level $\alpha$, with degrees of freedom $d.f. = n - 1$.
For a [[kw:right‑tailed test]]: use the chi‑square value that has area $\alpha$ to its right. In Google Sheets: `=CHISQ.INV.RT(α, d.f.)`.
For a [[kw:left‑tailed test]]: use the value that has area $\alpha$ to its left, i.e., right‑tail area $1 - \alpha$. In Google Sheets: `=CHISQ.INV(α, d.f.)` (cumulative from left).

For a [[kw:two‑tailed test]]: two critical values are needed. The lower value has area $\alpha/2$ to its left; the upper value has area $\alpha/2$ to its right. In Sheets: lower = `=CHISQ.INV(α/2, d.f.)`, upper = `=CHISQ.INV.RT(α/2, d.f.)`.
The chi‑square distribution is not symmetric, so the two critical values for a two‑tailed test are [[imp:not opposites]].

discoveryHook.scenario: A dairy company claims the variance of fat in its milk is at most 0.25. To test this, we need to know how large a sample variance would be too large. The chi‑square distribution provides the critical values that separate unusual sample variances from typical ones.

confusionCorner.title: Chi‑Square Critical Values Are Not Symmetric
confusionCorner.body: Unlike z‑tests and t‑tests, the critical values for a two‑tailed chi‑square test are [[imp:not opposites]]. The distribution is skewed, so the left and right cutoffs are different positive numbers.

explanation: The [[kw:chi‑square test statistic]] for a variance is: $$\chi^2 = \frac{(n-1)s^2}{\sigma^2_0}$$ where $\sigma^2_0$ is the hypothesized variance from $H_0$.
This statistic follows a chi‑square distribution with $d.f. = n-1$, provided the population is [[imp:normally distributed]].
If you are testing a standard deviation $\sigma$, square both the sample standard deviation and the hypothesized value: $\chi^2 = \frac{(n-1)s^2}{\sigma^2_0}$ (use variances).
The rejection region depends on $H_a$: right‑tailed if $H_a: \sigma^2 > \sigma^2_0$; left‑tailed if $H_a: \sigma^2 < \sigma^2_0$; two‑tailed if $H_a: \sigma^2 \neq \sigma^2_0$.
A large test statistic indicates the sample variance is larger than hypothesized; a small statistic indicates it is smaller.

teacherCues: Write the test statistic: $\chi^2 = \frac{(n-1)s^2}{\sigma^2_0}$. Compare to the z and t formulas.

discoveryHook.scenario: To test whether the variance of a process has increased, we compare the sample variance to the claimed variance using a ratio. If the sample variance is much larger than claimed, the test statistic will be large and may fall in the rejection region.

confusionCorner.title: Always Use Variances, Not Standard Deviations!
confusionCorner.body: The test statistic $\chi^2 = (n-1)s^2 / \sigma^2_0$ requires [[imp:variances]]. If the problem gives standard deviations, square them first. A common mistake is to plug in $s$ and $\sigma$ directly.

confusionCorner.title: Two‑Tailed P‑Value for Chi‑Square
confusionCorner.body: Because the chi‑square distribution is skewed, you cannot simply double the right‑tail area. [[imp:You must find both tail areas and double the smaller one.]] Google Sheets makes this easy.

hints: It returns the area in the right tail directly.
Similar to T.DIST.RT.

questions.prompt: For a two‑tailed chi‑square test, the P‑value is twice the ___ of the left‑tail and right‑tail areas.
A right‑tailed chi‑square test gives a P‑value of 0.015. At $\alpha = 0.05$, should you reject $H_0$? (Yes or No)
hints: Small P‑value indicates strong evidence against $H_0$.

explanation: The [[kw:P‑value]] for a chi‑square test is the probability of obtaining a $\chi^2$ statistic as extreme as, or more extreme than, the one computed, assuming $H_0$ is true.
Decision rule: If P‑value $\le \alpha$, reject $H_0$; otherwise, fail to reject.
In Google Sheets:
- Right‑tailed: `=CHISQ.DIST.RT(χ², d.f.)` — returns the area to the right.
- Left‑tailed: `=CHISQ.DIST(χ², d.f., TRUE)` — returns the cumulative area to the left.
- Two‑tailed: $2 \times$ the smaller of the left‑tail and right‑tail areas. For observed $\chi^2$, compute left area and right area; the P‑value = $2 \times \min(\text{left area, right area})$.
The chi‑square table typically only provides ranges for P‑values, so technology is especially helpful.

legend.meaning: The two‑tailed P‑value is not simply twice the right‑tail area because the distribution is skewed.

confusionCorner.title: Normality Is Critical
confusionCorner.body: The chi‑square test for a variance is highly sensitive to the normality assumption. If the population is not normal, the actual Type I error rate can be very different from $\alpha$. [[imp:Always check for approximate normality before using this test.]]

formulaCard.formula: $$\text{Right-tailed: reject if } \chi^2 > \chi^2_R$$ $$\text{Left-tailed: reject if } \chi^2 < \chi^2_L$$ $$\text{Two-tailed: reject if } \chi^2 < \chi^2_L \text{ or } \chi^2 > \chi^2_R$$

legend.meaning: Always compare the test statistic to the critical value(s) based on the direction of $H_a$.

formulaCard.title: Decision Rule Summary

rows.1: $56.25 > 50.892$ → reject $H_0$. The variance appears to exceed the claimed maximum.

explanation: Chi‑square tests for variances are commonly used in [[kw:quality control]] to monitor process consistency.
A right‑tailed test is often used to detect an [[imp:increase]] in variance (process deterioration).
A left‑tailed test can detect an [[imp:improvement]] (reduced variability).
A two‑tailed test checks whether the variance differs from a target value.
The test is [[imp:not robust]] to departures from normality. If the population is not normal, the results may be misleading.
When interpreting, remember that failing to reject $H_0$ does not prove the variance equals the claimed value; it only means the sample did not provide strong evidence against it.

visuals.title: Blueprint for Police Response Time Claim ($\alpha=0.05$)

explanation: Blueprint steps: [[imp:Understand → Solve → Conclude]].

1. [[kw:Understand]]: Verify the population is approximately normal. Identify the claim and write $H_0$ and $H_a$. Determine whether the test is right‑, left‑, or two‑tailed. Note $n$, $s$ (or $s^2$), and $\alpha$.

2. [[kw:Solve]]: Compute the test statistic $\chi^2 = \frac{(n-1)s^2}{\sigma^2_0}$ (square standard deviations if needed). Find the critical value(s) from the chi‑square table or Google Sheets. Compare the test statistic to the rejection region, or find the P‑value and compare to $\alpha$.
3. [[kw:Conclude]]: Make a decision and interpret in context. Use 'There is (or is not) enough evidence to support/reject the claim that…'.
